# Slide decks

Apply this skill when slides are needed for a talk, a pitch, a sprint demo, a steering committee or any review where someone presents to an audience.

## Start from the message

Write the storyline before opening PowerPoint, Keynote or Google Slides:

1. One sentence: what should the audience decide, believe or do after the talk?
2. Three to five supporting points, each of which becomes a section.
3. For each slide, an action title - a full sentence that states the point ("Churn fell 12% after the onboarding change"), not a topic label ("Churn").

If you read only the slide titles in order, they should tell the whole story. This is the classic "pyramid" or "horizontal logic" check.

## Slide rules

- One message per slide. Two messages, two slides.
- Body text supports the title; no paragraphs. If it needs paragraphs, it belongs in a handout or the speaker notes.
- At least 24 pt for body text, 32 pt or more for titles in a large room.
- Use the slide master and layouts; do not position title boxes by hand.
- Contrast and colour-blind-safe palettes; never red against green as the only distinction.

## Charts

| Data | Chart |
|---|---|
| Change over time | line chart |
| Comparison of categories | horizontal bar chart, sorted |
| Part of a whole, two or three parts | stacked bar; avoid pie with many slices |
| Relationship between two measures | scatter plot |

Remove gridlines, legends that can be replaced by direct labels, 3D effects and decimal places nobody needs. Highlight the one bar or line the title talks about and grey the rest.

## Speaker notes

Write in the notes what you will say, including numbers and sources, so the deck works for someone presenting it in your place and as a read-out afterwards. Put data sources and footnotes on the slide in small type when figures will be quoted.

## Before presenting

- [ ] Title-only read-through tells the story
- [ ] Every number checked against its source
- [ ] Animations only where they reveal steps in order
- [ ] Fonts embedded or standard; test on the presentation machine
- [ ] Exported PDF for people who cannot open the source format
- [ ] Timing rehearsed: roughly one to two minutes per slide

## Pitfalls

- Dense "eye chart" tables copied from a spreadsheet.
- An appendix that has become the main deck.
- Generated decks (python-pptx, Marp, reveal.js) that ignore the corporate template.

Workbook figures feeding the charts are built with spreadsheet-formulas. Architecture pictures come from diagramming, and the general file checklist is in documents.
